nameStory: The Slaty-backed Gull gets its name from the distinctive slate-gray coloring across its back and wings, which sets it apart from other large gulls. The word 'slaty' refers to the blue-gray color of slate rock, perfectly describing this bird's most recognizable feature.
description: The Slaty-backed Gull is a large, white-headed seabird that's a rare but exciting visitor to New England's coastlines. This robust gull is similar in size to the familiar Herring Gull but sports a distinctive slate-gray back that makes it stand out among flocks of more common gulls. Like other large gulls, it has a sturdy build, powerful wings, and a thick bill perfect for its opportunistic feeding habits.

idTips.label: Slate-gray back
idTips.description: The back and upper wings display a distinctive medium gray color, darker than a Herring Gull but lighter than a Great Black-backed Gull - imagine the color of a stormy sky

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Noticeably robust and heavy-bodied, similar in size to a Great Black-backed Gull with broad, powerful wings that create an imposing silhouette

idTips.label: White head and underparts
idTips.description: Clean white head, neck, chest, and belly that contrasts sharply with the gray back - the white appears bright and pristine in good light

idTips.label: Thick yellow bill
idTips.description: Heavy, robust yellow bill that looks substantial and powerful, often with a red spot near the tip that's visible at close range

idTips.label: Pink legs
idTips.description: Sturdy pinkish or flesh-colored legs that appear thick and strong, providing a stable base for this large bird

habitat: In New England, Slaty-backed Gulls are extremely rare visitors found almost exclusively along rocky coastlines, harbors, and large estuaries during winter months. They're most likely spotted mixing with flocks of other large gulls at fish processing plants, landfills near the coast, or roosting on piers and breakwaters.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England during spring as birds begin their journey back to breeding grounds in the North Pacific.
seasonality.summer: Essentially absent from New England during summer months when they're breeding on remote northern Pacific coasts.
seasonality.fall: Extremely rare fall visitor, with any sightings creating excitement among local birders as birds begin winter movements.
seasonality.winter: Peak time for rare sightings in New England, when a few individuals may join mixed gull flocks along the coast, particularly at reliable feeding sites.

funFact: Despite being spotted only 11 times in all of New England, each Slaty-backed Gull sighting here represents an incredible journey of over 3,000 miles from their normal Pacific Ocean range - that's like a bird from California somehow ending up in Maine!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Herring Gulls due to similar size and white head, but remember the Slaty-backed's distinctly darker gray back - think 'storm cloud gray' versus the Herring Gull's lighter 'pearl gray.' The size difference with smaller gulls like Ring-billed makes confusion with those species unlikely.
contextualKnowledge: This species is also sometimes called the 'Pacific Gull,' which can be confusing since there's a completely different Southern Hemisphere species with the same common name. Slaty-backed Gulls normally live around the northern Pacific Ocean, making any New England appearance a major rarity worth reporting to local birding communities.
compareHints: Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust. Unlike the Great Black-backed Gull, which has an almost black back, the Slaty-backed shows medium gray tones. It lacks the pale, almost white back of the Glaucous Gull, making the gray back coloration the key distinguishing feature among large white-headed gulls.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.
Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
